title: What are Stream Gatherers (Stream.gather, JEP 485), why were they needed, and what do they enable (windowing, batching, folding)?
shortTitle: Stream Gatherers (JEP 485, Java 24) — custom stateful intermediate operations

s1_definition.profdef: Gatherers (JEP 485, stable Java 24) are CUSTOM INTERMEDIATE OPERATIONS for streams — the intermediate counterpart to Collectors (which are terminal). `stream.gather(Gatherer)` lets you define stateful, one-to-many transformations in the middle of a pipeline. Built-in: `Gatherers.windowFixed(3)` creates fixed-size batches, `Gatherers.windowSliding(3)` creates sliding windows, `Gatherers.fold(init, fn)` accumulates state as an intermediate op. Needed because map/filter/flatMap are stateless one-to-one (or one-to-many) — they can't express "group every 3 elements into a sub-list" or "emit running totals" cleanly.
s1_definition.analogy: Collectors are like the FINAL packaging at the end of the assembly line (terminal). Gatherers are like INTERMEDIATE processing stations — "batch every 3 trades into a group" (windowFixed), "compute running balance after each trade" (fold), "look at each 3-trade window for patterns" (windowSliding). Before Gatherers, you needed ugly workarounds.
s1_definition.oneliner: Gatherers = custom intermediate ops. windowFixed(n) = batching. windowSliding(n) = sliding windows. fold(init, fn) = running state. Complement to Collectors (terminal).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Gatherers (JEP 485, stable Java 24) are CUSTOM INTERMEDIATE OPERATIONS for streams — the intermediate counterpart to Collectors (which are terminal). `stream.gather(Gatherer)` lets you define stateful, one-to-many transformations in the middle of a pipeline. Built-in: `Gatherers.windowFixed(3)` creates fixed-size batches, `Gatherers.windowSliding(3)` creates sliding windows, `Gatherers.fold(init, fn)` accumulates state as an intermediate op. Needed because map/filter/flatMap are stateless one-to-one (or one-to-many) — they can't express "group every 3 elements into a sub-list" or "emit running totals" cleanly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Collectors are like the FINAL packaging at the end of the assembly line (terminal). Gatherers are like INTERMEDIATE processing stations — "batch every 3 trades into a group" (windowFixed), "compute running balance after each trade" (fold), "look at each 3-trade window for patterns" (windowSliding). Before Gatherers, you needed ugly workarounds.

**One line to remember:** Gatherers = custom intermediate ops. windowFixed(n) = batching. windowSliding(n) = sliding windows. fold(init, fn) = running state. Complement to Collectors (terminal).

sections.s2_technical:
Stream Gatherers (JEP 485, finalised around Java 24) add CUSTOM stateful intermediate operations to the Stream API via `stream.gather(gatherer)`. Before gatherers, custom intermediate logic (sliding windows, running de-duplication, fixed-size batching) had no clean API — you fought with `reduce` or external state. A gatherer defines an initializer (state), an integrator (process element, maybe emit), an optional combiner (parallel), and an optional finisher (emit leftovers).

Built-in gatherers in `java.util.stream.Gatherers` include `windowFixed(n)` (group into fixed-size lists), `windowSliding(n)` (overlapping windows), `fold` (stateful reduction keeping intermediate results), and `scan` (prefix-accumulation emitting each step). For example `trades.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2)).toList()` batches trades two at a time for bulk settlement.

A banking example: computing a running balance after each transaction uses `Gatherers.scan(() -> start, (bal, txn) -> bal.add(txn.delta()))`, which emits the balance after every transaction — something `reduce` cannot do because it only yields the final value. Senior nuance: gatherers are to intermediate operations what collectors are to terminal operations; reach for them when you need stateful, possibly one-to-many intermediate processing that `map`/`filter`/`flatMap` cannot express.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Producing a running balance after EACH transaction was impossible with `reduce` (which only returns the final value) and ugly with external mutable state. Fix: a Stream Gatherer with `scan` emits the balance after every transaction as a proper stateful intermediate operation, and `windowFixed` batches transactions for bulk settlement.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: a stream of five transaction deltas 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.

**Step 2.** `gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2))` is a stateful intermediate operation that buffers elements into fixed-size windows.

**Step 3.** After every two elements it emits a batch: [10,20], then [30,40].

**Step 4.** The finisher emits the leftover final window [50] even though it is incomplete.

**Step 5.** The result is the batched list [[10,20],[30,40],[50]], ready for bulk settlement.

```text
INFO: batches=[[10, 20], [30, 40], [50]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ GATHERERS = CUSTOM INTERMEDIATE OPS ═══

  Before Gatherers:
    map/filter/flatMap = stateless, 1-to-1 or 1-to-many
    No way to: batch, window, fold as INTERMEDIATE ops
    Workaround: ugly IntStream.range + subList

  After Gatherers (Java 24):
    stream.gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(3))   → batching
    stream.gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(3)) → sliding window
    stream.gather(Gatherers.fold(init, fn))   → running accumulation

  Collectors = custom TERMINAL ops (end of pipeline)
  Gatherers = custom INTERMEDIATE ops (middle of pipeline)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream Gatherers (JEP 485, Java 24) fill the gap between map/filter (stateless intermediates) and Collectors (terminal). They enable custom stateful intermediate operations: windowFixed for batching, windowSliding for pattern detection, fold for running accumulations. Before Gatherers, these patterns required ugly workarounds with IntStream.range or external libraries. Gatherers complement Collectors: Collectors customize HOW you produce the final result (terminal), Gatherers customize HOW you process elements IN the pipeline (intermediate). If your interview targets Java 21 or earlier, mention Gatherers as "coming in Java 24."
